title: Picross DS
subtitle: A picture hidden inside a grid
summary: Picross DS is Jupiter's Nintendo DS collection of nonogram puzzles, where numbered clues describe the filled squares needed to reveal a picture. The player works between rows and columns, marking cells as occupied or empty until the image becomes clear. The stylus gives this quiet process a direct surface, while progressively larger puzzles demand more careful comparison. Each completed grid offers two kinds of satisfaction at once: the logic has been resolved and the apparently abstract marks have turned into something that can finally be recognised as a small image.
body: Picross DS is Jupiter's Nintendo DS collection of nonogram puzzles, where numbered clues describe the filled squares needed to reveal a picture. The player works between rows and columns, marking cells as occupied or empty until the image becomes clear. The stylus gives this quiet process a direct surface, while progressively larger puzzles demand more careful comparison. Each completed grid offers two kinds of satisfaction at once: the logic has been resolved and the apparently abstract marks have turned into something that can finally be recognised as a small image.

Numbers alongside a row or column describe groups of consecutive filled cells, with spaces separating one group from the next. Comparing the available length with those groups reveals where a square must belong or remain empty. A deduction in one direction can then resolve an uncertainty in the other. Normal mode identifies mistakes and adds time penalties, encouraging a careful reading before committing to a cell. The most useful action may be marking an empty square, because removing a possibility can provide the information needed to complete the next line.

Puzzle creation allows players to design their own pictures, while the original online features provided ways to share them, download classic grids and compete over solving speed. Daily challenges offer another short routine alongside the main collection. Difficulty grows through larger arrangements and more demanding relationships between clues, giving the same basic rule a substantial range. Picross DS makes the handheld useful as a small puzzle book, with the additional pleasure that an image devised by a player can become a problem for somebody else to solve.
